subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 56-year-old man with chronic pericardial disease is examined at the bedside. With each inspiration, the examiner observes that the patient's jugular venous pressure rises rather than falls, and the neck veins become more distended during the inspiratory phase of respiration.
question: Which of the following best describes this physical finding?

options.text: A paradoxical fall in systolic blood pressure of greater than 10 mm Hg during inspiration
A paradoxical rise in jugular venous pressure during inspiration
The normal fall in jugular venous pressure expected during inspiration
A prominent x descent reflecting rapid atrial emptying
An irregularly occurring cannon a wave from atrial contraction against a closed tricuspid valve

explanation_correct: Kussmaul sign is a paradoxical increase in jugular venous pressure on inspiration. Normally, inspiration creates negative intrathoracic pressure, which increases venous return to the right heart and decreases JVP. When right ventricular filling is impaired — as in constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, right heart failure, massive pulmonary embolism, or right atrial/ventricular tumors — the RV cannot accommodate the increased venous return, so blood backs up into the vena cava and the JVP rises during inspiration.

explanation_incorrect.A: A paradoxical inspiratory fall in systolic blood pressure greater than 10 mm Hg is pulsus paradoxus, a different finding seen classically in cardiac tamponade and severe asthma; Kussmaul sign refers to the jugular venous pressure, not the arterial pressure.
explanation_incorrect.C: A fall in JVP on inspiration is the normal response, precisely the opposite of this patient's paradoxical rise; calling the normal fall a finding would be a misstatement of the sign.
explanation_incorrect.D: The x descent is a component of the normal JVP waveform reflecting atrial relaxation and descent of the tricuspid valve during systole; it does not describe an inspiratory change in JVP.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cannon a waves occur irregularly when the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve (as in complete heart block or junctional rhythms); they are beat-to-beat waveform events, not an inspiratory JVP rise.

educationalObjective: Kussmaul sign is a paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration caused by impaired RV filling, classically seen in constrictive pericarditis and restrictive cardiomyopathy.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 58-year-old man is evaluated for progressive dyspnea and bilateral leg swelling over several months. Twenty years ago he received mantle radiation therapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. Examination shows distended neck veins that rise with inspiration, peripheral edema, and ascites. Auscultation reveals a brief early diastolic sound shortly after S2. Chest CT shows a thickened, partially calcified pericardium with normal ventricular size and systolic function.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Cardiac tamponade
Restrictive cardiomyopathy
Constrictive pericarditis
Tricuspid regurgitation
Right ventricular infarction

explanation_correct: Chronic pericardial inflammation leads to fibrosis with or without calcification, limiting the space for ventricular expansion and decreasing ventricular filling. The presentation — dyspnea, peripheral edema, jugular venous distention with Kussmaul sign, pulsus paradoxus, and a pericardial knock (the early diastolic sound) — is classic. Thoracic radiotherapy is a recognized late cause, and the calcified thickened pericardium with normal systolic function on CT confirms the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Cardiac tamponade is an acute process in which pericardial fluid compresses all chambers; it produces pulsus paradoxus prominently but does not cause a pericardial knock or a chronically calcified pericardium, and Kussmaul sign is a feature of constriction rather than tamponade.
explanation_incorrect.B: Restrictive cardiomyopathy also causes impaired filling and can show Kussmaul sign, but the CT evidence of a thickened, calcified pericardium with normal ventricular wall thickness points to an extrinsic pericardial cause; the radiation history can produce both, making the pericardial imaging decisive.
explanation_incorrect.D: Tricuspid regurgitation produces a holosystolic murmur, prominent v waves, and hepatic pulsation, but no pericardial knock, calcified pericardium, or pattern of equalized diastolic pressures.
explanation_incorrect.E: Right ventricular infarction is an acute ischemic event with abrupt right-sided failure and elevated JVP, but not a chronic months-long course with a calcified pericardium and pericardial knock.

educationalObjective: Constrictive pericarditis causes impaired ventricular filling from a fibrotic and often calcified pericardium, presenting with JVD, Kussmaul sign, pulsus paradoxus, and a pericardial knock; thoracic radiotherapy is a late cause.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 61-year-old man with a remote history of viral pericarditis presents with progressive dyspnea, abdominal distention, and leg swelling. Neck veins are markedly distended and rise with inspiration, and an early diastolic knock is heard. Echocardiography shows normal systolic function, a thickened pericardium, abrupt cessation of ventricular filling in early diastole with a plateau (dip-and-plateau), and exaggerated septal motion with respiration.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's elevated venous pressures?

options.text: Compression of all four cardiac chambers by a large pericardial effusion
Primary myocardial fibrosis that has destroyed contractile elements
Obstruction of the tricuspid valve by a right atrial tumor
A rigid, noncompliant pericardium that limits ventricular expansion and filling
Acute right ventricular pressure overload from a large pulmonary embolism

explanation_correct: In constrictive pericarditis, chronic inflammation of the pericardium produces fibrosis with or without calcification, which limits the space for expansion and thereby decreases ventricular filling. The reduced end-diastolic volume leads to decreased cardiac output and increased venous return backing up into the systemic veins, producing JVD, Kussmaul sign, edema, and ascites. The dip-and-plateau filling pattern, pericardial knock, and normal systolic function all reflect the rigid pericardial shell, not intrinsic myocardial disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Compression by fluid is tamponade physiology; this patient has a thickened rigid pericardium rather than a large effusion, and tamponade does not typically show the dip-and-plateau filling or pericardial knock of constriction.
explanation_incorrect.B: Myocardial fibrosis with loss of contractility would reduce systolic function, but this patient's systolic function is normal and the abnormality is filling, implicating the pericardium rather than the myocardium.
explanation_incorrect.C: A right atrial tumor can impair RV filling and cause Kussmaul sign, but the imaging here shows the pericardium itself as the problem; a tumor would be visible as a mass obstructing the valve, not a thickened shell.
explanation_incorrect.E: Massive pulmonary embolism acutely raises RV pressures and can produce a Kussmaul-type picture, but it presents abruptly with hypoxia and RV strain, not a chronic months-long syndrome with pericardial thickening.

educationalObjective: Constrictive pericarditis limits ventricular filling through a rigid, fibrotic pericardium, decreasing EDV and cardiac output while venous pressures rise — a filling problem with preserved systolic function.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 49-year-old recent immigrant from a country with a high burden of tuberculosis presents with months of progressive dyspnea, peripheral edema, and abdominal distention. Neck veins are distended and rise with inspiration. Chest CT shows pericardial thickening with dense calcification. Cardiac catheterization shows equalization of diastolic pressures in all four chambers.
question: In this patient's region of origin, which of the following is the most common cause of the pericardial process described?

options.text: Idiopathic and viral pericarditis
Prior cardiac surgery
Uremia
Rheumatoid arthritis
Tuberculosis

explanation_correct: This patient has constrictive pericarditis: chronic pericardial inflammation leading to fibrosis with calcification, limited ventricular filling, and equalization of diastolic pressures, with JVD and Kussmaul sign. Tuberculosis is the most common cause of constrictive pericarditis in resource-limited countries, matching this patient's origin; in resource-rich settings the usual causes are idiopathic or viral disease, cardiac surgery, and thoracic radiotherapy (late).

explanation_incorrect.A: Idiopathic and viral pericarditis are the usual causes of constriction in developed, resource-rich countries, not in areas with a high tuberculosis burden.
explanation_incorrect.B: Cardiac surgery is an important cause of constriction in resource-rich settings, but there is no surgical history here, and the geographic context points to tuberculosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Uremia causes acute (often effusive) pericarditis treated with dialysis; it is not a recognized leading cause of chronic calcific constriction.
explanation_incorrect.D: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease that can cause pericarditis, but it is not the most common cause of constrictive pericarditis in resource-limited countries.

educationalObjective: Tuberculosis is the most common cause of constrictive pericarditis in resource-limited countries, while idiopathic/viral disease, cardiac surgery, and late radiation dominate in resource-rich settings.
